title: Petra and the Atlas
premise: In 1848, in a printing quarter on the brink of uprising, Paloma Delacroix works her father's type cases and keeps her head down—until a sealed letter arrives naming the Delacroix family as holders of a promise made to a man now branded an enemy of the state. The letter demands they deliver an atlas of hand-cut maps, engraved years ago in peacetime, to its exiled owner before the century's borders close forever. As revolution ignites and soldiers search the print shops, Paloma must choose between the family's safety and the debt of memory, discovering along the way that the atlas hides more than maps—it holds the truth of who she really is. She delivers it at terrible cost, losing her father's shop but gaining a name, a history, and a place she finally belongs.
about_author: Freya Nystrom is the pen name of a former bookbinder's apprentice who spent a decade restoring nineteenth-century ledgers in northern archives. She writes about the quiet hands behind loud histories.

chapters.title: The Weight of Lead
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. We meet the Delacroix print shop: her father cutting typefaces, Paloma setting pages by lamplight, both careful to be unremarkable in a city simmering with unrest. Emotional beat: the comfort of routine and small, invisible lives.

chapters.title: A Letter Under Seal
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. A courier delivers a sealed letter addressed not to her father but to 'the keeper of the Atlas.' Her father goes pale and burns nothing fast enough. Emotional beat: dread cracking open a settled world.

chapters.title: What Father Burned
chapters.summary: Father's POV. He recalls, obliquely, the summer he engraved maps for a foreign cartographer—a friend from before borders meant anything—and the promise exchanged over brandy. Emotional beat: guilt and tenderness entangled.

chapters.title: The Empty Drawer
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Searching for the atlas, she finds the drawer empty except for a brass key stamped with a compass rose. Emotional beat: the first thrill of a secret that is hers alone.

chapters.title: Soldiers at the Door
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. A government inspector questions printers about seditious material; the family's name appears on a list. Father lies smoothly; Paloma realizes invisibility was always a performance. Emotional beat: fear sharpening into awareness.

chapters.title: The Compass Rose
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The key fits a locker in the old guildhall library, where the atlas waits—hand-colored maps of a country that no longer exists on any current chart. Emotional beat: wonder, and the vertigo of holding something dangerous and beautiful.

chapters.title: Pages That Shouldn't Exist
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Studying the atlas at night, she finds marginal notes in her father's hand—and one signature that isn't his: her mother's, dead ten years, listed as co-engraver. Emotional beat: grief rekindled into questions.

chapters.title: Mother's Hand
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Mother's POV. The peacetime summer of engraving: three friends, one atlas, a promise that the finished work would reach the cartographer's daughter someday. Emotional beat: warmth shadowed by what the reader knows is coming.

chapters.title: The Name on the List
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She learns the promised recipient, Véra Lindqvist, has been declared an enemy agent; contact means treason. A neighbor informs on the shop. Emotional beat: loyalty and survival pulling apart.

chapters.title: Riot in the Print Quarter
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Revolution erupts; presses are smashed or seized, ink runs in gutters like spilled blood. The Delacroix shop survives by a hair. Emotional beat: chaos making every choice urgent.

chapters.title: What We Owe the Dead
chapters.summary: Father and Paloma argue. He wants to burn the atlas; she refuses—the promise was made to her mother too. Emotional beat: the first true rupture between them, love expressed as anger.

chapters.title: The Forger's Favor
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She seeks out Cazal, an aging forger who owed her father money, to alter travel papers. He agrees—for a price: one page of the atlas. Emotional beat: uneasy bargaining, moral grayness.

chapters.title: Disguised as Cargo
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The atlas travels hidden in a crate of type sorts; Paloma follows disguised as a printer's errand girl. First checkpoint passed. Emotional beat: tense momentum, growing competence.

chapters.title: Cazal's Price
chapters.summary: Cazal's POV. He copies the map page and hesitates—he knows what such borders are worth to men who redraw countries. Emotional beat: conscience flickering in a compromised man.

chapters.title: The Road East
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. On the road she falls in with refugees and hears stories of the displaced; the atlas's vanished country becomes real through their voices. Emotional beat: empathy deepening purpose into conviction.

chapters.title: Intercepted
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Soldiers seize the crate at a ferry crossing. Paloma escapes with only the atlas's final page sewn into her coat. Emotional beat: despair, then grim resolve.

chapters.title: The Last Page
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Deciphering the final page, she finds a hidden dedication revealing her mother planned the delivery all along—and that Véra Lindqvist is her godmother. Emotional beat: identity remade in a single revelation.

chapters.title: Betrayal in the Archive
chapters.summary: Cazal's copied page surfaces; the inspector traces the route and closes in. A sympathetic archivist warns Paloma at great risk. Emotional beat: hunted, betrayed, but no longer alone.

chapters.title: Crossing the Line
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Climax begins: she crosses the border at night with the last page, pursued, guided by a refugee whose village appears on her mother's maps. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into courage.

chapters.title: Véra
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. In a snowbound house she meets Véra Lindqvist, old and sharp-eyed, who recognizes her mother's hand before her face. The page completes the atlas. Emotional beat: recognition, belonging, tears.

chapters.title: The Century Turns
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. The inspector arrives; Véra's standing and the completed atlas—proof of a peaceable friendship between nations—turn the accusation hollow. Father arrives to take Paloma home. Emotional beat: release, reconciliation, justice without triumph.

chapters.title: Setting New Type
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, epilogue tone. The shop rebuilt smaller; Paloma cuts her first original typeface and signs the atlas's printed dedication with both her names—the one she was given and the one she found. Emotional beat: quiet, earned belonging.
